1	# Task 11: Solar-system explorer with focus on click
2	
3	Build a single-page browser app with the provided framework, served by vite, rendering to the canvas with id #app. The app is an interactive, stylised solar system explorer on a dark starfield background.
4	
5	Show a glowing central star and at least 6 planets, each at a different orbital distance, with a different size and colour and orbiting the star at a different speed (inner planets faster). At least one planet has a moon orbiting it, and at least one planet has a ring. Draw a thin circular orbit line for each planet. Planets should also spin about their own axis. Use a simple procedural look (colour, gradients or generated textures); do not load external assets from the network.
6	
7	The user can click a planet to focus on it. On focus, the camera smoothly moves (about 1.5 seconds, eased) to a close view of that planet and keeps following it as it orbits, and a DOM info panel appears showing the planet's name, its orbital period in Earth days, and its distance from the star in million km. Clicking empty space, or pressing the Escape key, smoothly returns to the overview showing the whole system and hides the panel. In the overview, the user can drag to orbit the camera around the system and scroll to zoom within sensible limits. Add a toggle button labelled 'Pause' that stops and resumes orbital motion, and shows 'Play' while paused.
8	
9	The scene must look correct on first load with no console errors. Expose

I'm weighing whether mutating app.scene.camera as a plain spec would actually get picked up by the renderer, or if app.scene is just a frozen snapshot that won't do anything useful.

Instead I'm working out a world-group approach: keep the camera fixed and instead transform a parent group containing everything, using nested single-axis rotation groups (outer pitch, inner yaw) to avoid Euler order ambiguity, with translation handling the focus target and distance, while keeping background stars outside the group as a static layer.

For picking, I realize I don't need the engine's raycast -- I can project planet positions through my own view matrix and compare against screen-space radii directly.

Since I'm computing planet positions myself anyway and setting them via runtime handles, I don't need to rely on built-in picking logic at all; the groups just need setPosition/setRotation support at runtime, which matches patterns I've seen work before (like the robot sample with nested mutable group handles).

One nagging concern though: if I put a point light inside a transformed group to represent a star, I'm not certain the light actually inherits the group's parent transforms correctly at runtime. It might be safer to keep lighting outside the groups entirely and use a directional or hemisphere light to shade the planets instead, even though that's visually flatter.

I'm realizing the controller update order means my overrides apply one frame late, causing minor jitter as the planet moves — probably negligible, but a cleaner fix would be registering my own continuous rig that computes pose directly from my current state at update time rather than patching after the fact.

For initialization, I need the rig's starting pose to match the overview camera pose before I take over, and the rig type needs to supply up, roll, fov, near, and far. A simpler alternative is just calling setPose with partial overrides each frame instead of a full custom rig.

I'll run my simulation logic inside app.onFrame and let the rig's update just return the current pose variable, accepting a one-frame lag since ordering isn't critical here. For interaction, I'll handle pointer and wheel events directly on the canvas myself -- drag for orbit, wheel for zoom, and a short low-movement pointerup counts as a click for picking planets via my own screen projection.

For picking, I'll project each planet's center using the camera's lookAt and perspective parameters, compute its screen-space radius from depth and field of view, and treat a click as a hit if it falls within that radius (with a minimum clickable size so small planets stay selectable), picking the nearest one when multiple overlap. The star itself won't be clickable, acting as empty space for unfocus, and moons are excluded from picking too. I also need to expose a read-only `__TASK_STATE__` on window, which I'll do using defineProperty getters so test harnesses can inspect state without mutating it.

Now I'm sketching the solar system's physical layout: orbit radii, planet sizes, and real-world distances/periods scaled down, with angular speeds stylized so inner planets visibly orbit faster than outer ones rather than using true orbital mechanics (which would make outer planets nearly static).

I settle on a slower base speed so orbits take a reasonable number of seconds to complete, from Mercury at roughly 14s to Neptune taking several minutes, and start thinking through how the follow camera should trail a planet -- positioning itself offset to the side and slightly elevated, with distance scaled to the planet's radius.

I realize putting the camera directly behind the planet relative to the star would show its unlit dark side, so I need to offset tangentially instead, keeping the camera on the star-lit side while still trailing the orbit.

Rotating the radial direction by 60° and blending with elevation gives a nice half-lit view. I'm checking the math so the camera distance is far enough to keep Saturn's rings fully in frame at a 45° vertical field of view.

For the camera motion, I'm setting up a smooth easing transition between poses—blending from the current camera position and target toward a moving goal pose over 1.5 seconds using cubic easing, recalculating the goal each frame so it keeps following the planet during orbit.

I want this transition to use real elapsed time so it keeps working even when paused, but I need to cap the delta time since a low-fps test environment could otherwise stretch or distort the 1.5s duration.

For dragging and scrolling, I'll ignore those inputs entirely while focused — they should only affect the orbital overview camera. I'm also working out the initial overview framing: given a 45° fov and the system's outer radius, I need a pitch angle around 40° so the whole system is visible vertically.

Now I'm checking the zoom limits (60-320) and near/far planes against planet sizes at overview distance — mercury ends up tiny (around 2px radius), so clicking it needs a larger invisible hit area, or I should bump up the visual scale of inner planets a bit to make them clickable.

I'll stylize planet sizes: Mercury 1.2, Venus 2.0, Earth 2.2, Mars 1.6, Jupiter 5.0, Saturn 4.2, Uranus 3.0, Neptune 2.9, with star radius 7 and orbit radii stepping from 16 out to about 102. I'm adjusting the overview camera distance to around 230 with a 0.75 pitch so Neptune's orbit still fits vertically, and raising the max zoom to 380 with a far plane of 2000. I also want thin circular orbit lines drawn for each planet.

For the orbit rings, I'm weighing options between using a thin torus primitive versus a custom line-loop geometry, but since the material system may not render unlit lines reliably, a thin torus is probably the safer choice -- I need to check the exact parameter semantics for torus primitives.

I'm uncertain about the torus's default orientation in three.js, so rather than fight that ambiguity, I'll just build my own custom ring geometry for the orbit line instead.

Building the duplicated vertex geometry with flipped normals for both ring faces, not worrying too much about winding correctness since emissive shading hides backface darkness. I'll reuse this same double-sided annulus approach for Saturn's ring, just with inner/outer radii and banded vertex colors.

For the ring coloring, I'm planning a generic annulus helper that takes radial subdivisions and a color function, producing radial bands with per-vertex colors interpolated between inner and outer stops, multiplied across several radial steps for smoother banding. Orbit lines can reuse this with radialSteps=1 and a constant color, while lit rings like Saturn's get illuminated by the star's point light depending on the viewing angle.

I'm leaning toward pbr materials with white base color and vertex colors, keeping the ring as a separate node whose position tracks the planet each frame while its tilt rotation is set once and left static.

For the star's light source, I need a point light with intensity and decay calibrated properly—since these aren't three.js-calibrated, I should check whether setting decay to 0 (no falloff) is valid in the lighting implementation, since physically accurate decay would make the light too dim at any real distance.

I'm thinking through the decay and intensity defaults for point lights, considering using decay 0 with intensity around 4 to match the calibration I used for directional lights.

I'll add a low ambient/hemisphere fill light (around 0.25-0.35) so night sides of planets aren't pure black, skip shadows for simplicity, and look into whether there's a built-in helper like material.solarSun or material.solarCorona for creating the glowing star effect with emissive materials and a halo, checking how solar.js handles planet presets.

For rotation, I'll just spin each planet node around its own y-axis, which combined with the color variation will make the spin visually obvious without needing texture mapping. I'm working out the sphere geometry math now—computing vertex positions from spherical coordinates, normals as the normalized positions, and indices with correct winding so faces point outward, plus packing RGBA vertex colors into a flat array.

To hide the seam where longitude wraps around, I'll color each vertex based on its 3D position using a hash-based noise function rather than UV coordinates, so the color varies continuously and no visible seam forms at u=0/u=1.

For planet styles, I'm defining distinct coloring rules: gas giants get latitude bands with noise distortion, rocky planets get blotchy noise between two base colors, Earth gets blue oceans with noise-thresholded green continents and white polar caps, Venus gets a yellowish swirl, and Mars gets reddish-ochre tones with polar caps.

I'm also adding a small gray moon orbiting Earth at roughly 4.5 units radius with a fast ~5s orbital period.

I'm giving Jupiter two moons and Earth one, positioning each moon relative to its planet with a slight orbital tilt, and skipping separate orbit lines for moons since those are only drawn for planets. For the star, I'm considering an emissive sphere with a glow halo, possibly using a bloom post-processing effect (intensity ~0.8, threshold ~0.9) for a convincing glow, and thinking about whether to add surface granulation via vertex colors on the star's emissive material.

Deciding to use a plain emissive sphere (diameter 14) in warm orange/gold tones plus a slightly larger transparent corona sphere with low opacity for the glow, disabling shadow casting on the star. I'm also planning the starfield background with a dark navy scene color and scattered small instanced shapes on a large background sphere, making sure the camera's far clipping plane is set generously beyond that radius.

Working out star sizing so instances read as roughly 1-2px points at typical viewing distance, using plain white emissive material since instance tinting won't affect emissive color, with scale variation between instances and no fog since stars are self-lit and unaffected by scene lighting.

For the UI, I'll build the info panel and pause button directly in JS with inline styles rather than editing index.html, positioning them absolutely over the canvas so they don't interfere with canvas-only click listeners.

I'm setting the panel's pointer-events to none so clicks pass through to the canvas underneath, while keeping the button clickable in its corner. For input handling, I'm using pointerdown/pointerup on the canvas to distinguish clicks from drags based on movement distance, with pointer capture for reliable tracking, plus a window keydown listener for Escape.

I'm normalizing click coordinates using the canvas's bounding rect since the internal resolution matches CSS size, and computing aspect ratio from the rect dimensions to match the engine's vertical FOV convention. I'm also clamping camera pitch to avoid gimbal issues near the up vector.

One frame of lag means a small positional mismatch between camera pose and planet position—roughly 0.1 units of drift per frame for Mercury's angular speed against a camera distance of about 7 units, which seems small enough to not cause visible jitter.

Actually, I realize a cleaner fix: moving the position computation inside rig.update itself so pose and planet positions stay consistent within the same tick, since the controller runs before render anyway.

I'm working out the elevation angle and checking the star won't awkwardly block the view, then considering the easing logic: using easeInOutCubic to lerp from a saved starting state to the goal, snapping exactly to the goal when the transition completes, and making sure interrupted transitions correctly capture the current position as the new "from" state.
